one_liner: Community D (ldc2) solution to the related-posts benchmark, about 1.43x faster than the suite's C++ solution single-core.
what_it_does: A roughly 100-line D program (d_v2/source/app.d) that reads posts with tags, builds a tag-to-posts index, counts shared tags per post pair and keeps the top 5 related posts per post, then writes JSON. It is a benchmark entry, not a library: there is no API to call, but genRelatedPosts is a self-contained @safe function you could lift. JSON goes through asdf 0.7.17, outside the timed region.
how_it_is_fast: Same algorithm as cpp/main.cpp (tag index, uint8 shared-tag counters, 64-byte chunk filter, insertion top-5). The tag index stores pointers to the counter bytes (SharedCount*), taken once with a bounds-checked &counts[i], so the hot increment loop is ptr[0]++ with no per-increment bounds check, while the C++ entry increments through std::vector::at(). The increment loop is unrolled 11 wide, the 64-byte chunk filter is a plain foreach over a static array that the compiler can auto-vectorize, and counter reset is fused into the top-5 scan (chunk[] = 0 while the line is in cache) instead of a separate memset per post.
when_to_use: As a reference pattern for sparse co-occurrence counting (posts by tags, items by features) where one post's counters fit in L1/L2 (tens of thousands of entries)
When a D codebase needs bounds-checked (@safe, no -release) code that still avoids per-element checks in a hot scatter loop: hoist the check into pointer creation
Single-core batch jobs of 5k to 60k items with 4-5 tags each from a 28-tag vocabulary, the measured shape
When end-to-end memory matters: the raw results show about 118 MB peak RSS at 60k posts versus about 460 MB for the C++ entry
when_not_to_use: As evidence that D beats C++: the same pointer, unroll and fused-reset tricks are expressible in standard C++; the C++ entry simply does not use them
Small inputs: at 5k posts it is at parity with C++ (12.06 vs 12.20 ms, C++ timer has 1 ms resolution) and slower than Rust (9.84 ms)
Workloads with more than 255 shared tags per pair: counters are ubyte and would wrap (the suite caps tags at 100 per post)
Concurrent or highly optimised settings: the suite's separate tables (D Concurrent v2, D HO) apply, and D HO at 163.89 ms is about 3x slower than Rust HO at 51.55 ms
Library integration: it is a benchmark program with hard-coded ../posts.json paths and a GC-allocated result array

integration.dependencies: D runtime and GC (Phobos); asdf 0.7.17 with mir-algorithm 3.21.0 and mir-core 1.6.0 for JSON I/O only
integration.min_toolchain: ldc2 1.41.0 via dub (as measured, -O3 inlining, no -release); other D compilers not tested by the suite
integration.platforms: any ldc2 target; measured on x86-64 (AWS c7a.xlarge) without -march
integration.thread_safety: single-threaded; a separate d_con_v2 variant exists for the multicore table

gotchas: Rule asymmetry behind the speedup: the C++ hot increment was switched from raw pointer arithmetic to taggedPostCount.at() in commit 6104965 ('[cpp] use at', Oct 2023), and issue #350 rejected D's .ptr indexing for the same loop (Oct 2023), yet D v2 (Nov 2023) gets unchecked increments by storing GC-held element pointers in @safe code. It is within the suite's letter, but a C++ entry storing uint8_t* would remove the same checks.

C++ and D (v2) rows come from separate container runs (C++ 2026-02-24, D 2026-02-11), and the 20k and 60k posts.json files are regenerated by gen_fake_posts.py with an unseeded random generator for every run, so the two rows were timed on different random datasets of the same distribution; verify.py checks output only on the 5k round.

Despite the 'SWAR optimization' description in dub.json there is no SWAR; and D still does one associative-array lookup per tag per post in the timed loop, which C++ avoids by pre-resolving tag vectors.

When fewer than 5 posts share a tag, D leaves the remaining related slots as empty default Posts while C++ fills them with post 0; never triggered by the suite's data but the outputs differ in that edge case.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Among the same-suite siblings it has the best single-core total (1.10 s versus Rust 1.23 s and C3 1.28 s), mainly from the 60k round; pick the Rust entry instead for the smallest inputs (9.84 ms at 5k) or if you want the faster Rust HO variant, and treat all three as implementation comparisons rather than language results.
verified_claims_summary: On an AWS c7a.xlarge (CPU model not stated), mean processing time without JSON I/O was 12.06 / 122.21 / 961.08 ms for 5k / 20k / 60k posts (10, 3 and 3 runs) for D v2 built with ldc2 1.41.0 at -O3 with bounds checks on, versus 12.2 / 164.33 / 1393 ms for the C++ entry built with Arch Linux clang++ -O3 -std=c++20 (no -march, clang version unstated), about 1.43x on the totals (derived from page data). End to end including asdf versus nlohmann/json, the raw results show about 1.60 s versus 3.35-3.40 s and 118 MB versus 460 MB at 60k posts.
status_note: The suite (now served as zupat/related_post_gen, 500 stars, MIT) is maintained, with C++ results refreshed 2026-02-24, but the d_v2 directory has had no commits since Feb 2024; it is a copyable reference pattern, not a maintained library.
